mainTopic: Vows tied to the rains and to the month of אדר: does the wording 'until the rain' or 'until the rains' change when the vow ends, and which אדר does plain 'Adar' mean in a leap year?
overview: Just before this, רבי זירא explained that a vow 'until the rain' depends on the date when the second rainfall is supposed to come. The גמרא challenges him from a ברייתא in which רבי מאיר, רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי argue about the dates of the three רביעות. Through an earlier discussion, the גמרא shows that the second רביעה matters for a נודר. It also shows that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who counts seven days of real rain as the first and second רביעה, follows רבי יוסי. This seems to prove that the vow depends on actual rain. The גמרא answers that this ברייתא is about someone who said 'until the rains' (plural), so רבי זירא's rule stands. Then a new משנה teaches that a vow 'for a year' includes the extra month of a leap year, and that plain 'Adar' means the first אדר. The גמרא asks whether this follows only רבי יהודה, who says plain 'Adar' in a שטר means the first אדר. אביי answers that it can follow רבי מאיר too: רבי מאיר speaks of someone who knew it was a leap year, and our משנה is about someone who did not know.

steps.title: The objection begins: dates of the three rainfalls according to רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens an objection by quoting a ברייתא that lists the expected dates of the three rainfall periods.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: When is the time of the rainfall? The early one is on the third, the middle one on the seventh, and the late one on the twenty-third. These are the words of רבי מאיר. רבי יהודה says: on the seventh, the seventeenth, and the twenty-third.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge to רבי זירא by quoting a ברייתא about when the rains are expected. The actual attack comes only at the end, so for now just collect the information.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא splits the rainy season into three expected times, called רביעה. רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה each give three dates in the month of מרחשון. The point of the objection will come out only after the גמרא connects these dates to the case of a vow.

keyTerms.meaning: A rainfall period that soaks the ground
Early (the first rainfall)
Middle (the second rainfall)
Late (the third rainfall)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
When is the time of the rainfall?
The early one — on the third,
phrases.notes: All these dates are days of the month מרחשון.

phrases.english: the middle one — on the seventh,
the late one — on the twenty-third,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
On the seventh, on the seventeenth, and on the twenty-third.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a challenge against רבי זירא's preceding statement about a vow 'until the rain'.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's view that a vow 'until the rain' depends on the expected date of the second רביעה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This step only sets up the ברייתא. Steps 3-5 build the connection, and the attack lands in step 6.

steps.title: רבי יוסי's dates and his rule about when individuals fast
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues with רבי יוסי's dates, the latest of the three opinions, and his rule that individuals do not fast before ראש חודש כסלו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: on the seventeenth, on the twenty-third, and in the month of כסלו. And so too רבי יוסי would say: individuals do not fast until ראש חודש כסלו arrives.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a third opinion, from רבי יוסי, about the rainfall dates. It adds that special individuals do not start fasting for rain before ראש חודש כסלו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבי יוסי's view the first two rainfalls are on the 17th and 23rd of מרחשון, about a week apart. His third rainfall is at the start of כסלו. That is why he says fasting for lack of rain starts only then. Keep the week-long gap in mind, because it becomes the key in step 6.

keyTerms.meaning: Individuals: special people who fast for rain before the rest of the community
Fast
The first day of the month of כסלו

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
On the seventeenth, and on the twenty-third,
and in the month of Kislev.
And so too Rabbi Yosei would say:
The individuals do not fast
phrases.notes: These are especially pious people who fast for rain earlier than everyone else.

phrases.english: until the New Moon of Kislev arrives.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a third opinion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יוסי, the rainfalls are on the 17th and 23rd of מרחשון and at the start of כסלו, and individuals begin fasting only at ראש חודש כסלו.

steps.title: Why does the date of the second rainfall matter?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls an earlier discussion on this ברייתא. The first rainfall matters for asking for rain and the third for fasting, but what is the second one for?
steps.simpleTranslation: And we said about this: It makes sense that the first rainfall matters, for asking for rain. The third matters for fasting. But what does the second matter for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back an earlier discussion about this ברייתא. It asks what practical difference the date of the second rainfall makes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each date should have a practical use. The first tells us when to ask for rain in תפילה, and the third tells us when to fast if no rain has come. The second has no obvious use, so the question opens the door to connecting it with vows.

keyTerms.meaning: And we said about it (recalling an earlier discussion)
It makes sense / granted
To ask (for rain in prayer)
For what purpose?

phrases.english: And we said about this:
Granted, the first rainfall — it is for asking.
The third — it is for fasting.
But the second — for what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the practical use of the dates listed in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical law depends on the date of the second רביעה?

steps.title: רבי זירא: the second rainfall matters for someone who made a vow
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא answers that the date of the second rainfall matters for a person who vowed 'until the rain'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי זירא said: It is for someone who makes a vow.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers the question. The expected date of the second rainfall decides when a vow 'until the rain' ends.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ties the ברייתא's argument about dates to our משנה about a נודר. Now the different opinions about the second rainfall date decide when the vow ends. That link lets the next step pull a ruling about vows out of a ברייתא about rain.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who makes a vow

phrases.english: And Rabbi Zeira said:
For one who vows.
phrases.notes: He means someone who vowed 'until the rain'. Its end depends on the expected date of the second rainfall.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The date of the second רביעה decides when a vow 'until the rain' ends.

steps.title: Whose view is רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's rule about seven days of rain?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls a further question: which תנא does the ברייתא follow in which seven straight days of rain count as both the first and second rainfall?
steps.simpleTranslation: And we said about this: Whose view does this ברייתא follow? רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: rains that fell for seven days in a row, you count them as the first and the second rainfall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ruling of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל about rain that actually fell. It asks which of the three opinions above this ruling fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל talks about rain that really came down, seven days in a row, and counts it as two rainfalls. If one of the three opinions fits a seven-day gap between the first and second rainfall, then that opinion also counts real rain. The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose view does it follow?
One after another, in a row
Count

phrases.english: And we said about this:
In accordance with whom is that which was taught,
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:

phrases.aramaic: גְּשָׁמִים שֶׁיָּרְדוּ שִׁבְעָה יָמִים זֶה אַחַר זֶה —
phrases.english: Rains that fell for seven days, one after another —
you count them as
the first and second rainfall.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמְרִינַן עֲלַהּ: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion by tying another ברייתא to one of the opinions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which of the three תנאים does רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's seven-day rule match?

steps.title: It follows רבי יוסי, so actual rain counts, which challenges רבי זירא
steps.stepSummary: The answer is רבי יוסי. This shows that actual rain is counted for the second rainfall, which contradicts רבי זירא's view that only the expected date matters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל follows רבי יוסי. This answer is the punch line of the objection against רבי זירא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only רבי יוסי has the first and second rainfall about a week apart (the 17th and the 23rd). So רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who follows him, counts rain that actually fell as the first and second רביעה. Since the second רביעה is what matters for the נודר, his vow seems to depend on real rain, not on the calendar date as רבי זירא said.

keyTerms.meaning: In accordance with whom?

steps.whatToRemember: The second רביעה matters for a נודר. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, following רבי יוסי, counts actual rain as the first and second רביעה. That suggests the vow depends on real rain, which challenges רבי זירא.
steps.confusionAlert: The question 'כמאן' here is not just a side note about who said what. Its answer is the actual weapon against רבי זירא.

phrases.english: In accordance with whom? In accordance with Rabbi Yosei!
phrases.notes: In רבי יוסי's dates, the first two rainfalls are about a week apart, matching the seven days of rain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 5 and completes the objection begun in step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל follows רבי יוסי.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's view that a vow 'until the rain' depends on the expected date
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If actual rain falling counts as the second רביעה, and the second רביעה decides the vow, then the vow depends on real rain and not just on the calendar date.

steps.title: That ברייתא is about someone who said 'until the rains'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the contradiction with רבי זירא. The ברייתא that counts actual rain deals with a person who said 'until the rains,' in the plural.
steps.simpleTranslation: That ברייתא is about someone who said: 'Until the rains.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 6 and defends רבי זירא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא said that a vow 'until the rain' depends on the expected date. The ברייתא that counts actual rainfall is a different case: the person said 'until the rains,' which points to real rain falling. Different wording leads to a different result, so the two sources do not clash.

keyTerms.meaning: That one, here meaning that ברייתא
Until the rains (plural), which means actual rainfall

steps.whatToRemember: In vows the exact wording matters. 'Until the rain' goes by the expected date, while 'until the rains' goes by when rain actually falls.

phrases.english: That one is where he said "until the rains."
phrases.notes: Notice the plural, 'rains.' That word is the whole answer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 6
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the cases by the wording of the vow
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא that counts actual rain seemed to contradict רבי זירא's rule that only the expected date matters
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about 'until the rains,' which refers to actual rain. רבי זירא's rule about the date still stands for 'until the rain.'

steps.title: New משנה: vows for a year, and vows until אדר in a leap year
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a vow 'for a year' includes the extra month of a leap year, and that 'until the beginning or end of Adar' means the first אדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone says 'Wine is קונם for me, I will not taste it for a year,' and the year becomes a leap year, wine is forbidden to him for the year and its added month. If he said 'until the beginning of Adar,' the vow lasts until the beginning of the first אדר. If he said 'until the end of Adar,' it lasts until the end of the first אדר.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It explains how a leap year affects vows tied to a year or to the month אדר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow 'for a year' covers the whole year, so the added month is included too. When the person just says 'Adar' and gives no detail, the משנה reads it as the first אדר, which is the first one he reaches.

keyTerms.meaning: A word for a vow that makes something forbidden like a קרבן
The year was made a leap year, with an extra month added
Its added month
The first אדר in a leap year

steps.confusionAlert: In a leap year there are two months of אדר. The משנה says that plain 'Adar' means the FIRST one, not the second.

phrases.english: MISHNA
"Wine is konam for me, that I will not taste it for a year,"
if the year was made a leap year,
he is forbidden during it and during its added month.
"Until the beginning of Adar":
until the beginning of the first Adar.
"Until the end of Adar":
until the end of the first Adar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the rain discussion is finished
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow for a year includes the leap month. 'Adar' with no detail means the first אדר.

steps.title: Inference: plain 'Adar' means the first אדר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws a general rule from the משנה: when a person says 'Adar' without specifying, he means the first אדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: So we see that plain 'Adar,' when someone says it, means the first אדר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pulls a general principle out of the משנה. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה ruled about a vow. The גמרא turns that ruling into a wider rule about how people speak: an unspecified 'Adar' refers to the first אדר. That wider rule is what the next step will compare with a מחלוקת.

keyTerms.meaning: So we see; this introduces an inference
Plain, with nothing specified

phrases.english: GEMARA
Apparently, a plain "Adar"
that a person says means the first one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general rule from the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Unspecified 'Adar' refers to the first אדר.

steps.title: Does the משנה follow only רבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the משנה follows רבי יהודה. In a ברייתא about dating documents, רבי יהודה holds that plain 'Adar' means the first אדר, and רבי מאיר holds that it means the second.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say the משנה follows רבי יהודה? As we learned in a ברייתא: in the first אדר, one writes 'the first Adar'; in the second אדר, one writes plain 'Adar.' These are the words of רבי מאיר. רבי יהודה says: in the first אדר one writes plain 'Adar,' and in the second אדר one writes 'second.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether the משנה matches only one side of a מחלוקת, the side of רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי מאיר, plain 'Adar' is the second אדר, because that is what one writes in the second month. For רבי יהודה, plain 'Adar' is the first. Since the משנה reads plain 'Adar' as the first, it seems to follow רבי יהודה and not רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say; this offers a suggestion to be checked
Second (Aramaic)
He writes, here meaning when dating a שטר

steps.whyThisMatters: A לימא question usually means the גמרא would rather not leave the משנה as only one side of a מחלוקת. So expect it to try to fit רבי מאיר as well.

phrases.english: Shall we say our mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda?
As it was taught:
In the first Adar, one writes "the first Adar";
phrases.notes: This is about writing the date on a שטר.

phrases.english: in the second Adar, one writes plain "Adar";
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
in the first Adar, one writes it plain;
in the second Adar, one writes "second."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the inference from Step 9 against a ברייתא with a מחלוקת
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the משנה follows only רבי יהודה and goes against רבי מאיר

steps.title: אביי: The משנה Can Follow רבי מאיר Too
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the משנה can follow even רבי מאיר. The ברייתא, where רבי מאיר says 'Adar' means the second אדר, is about someone who knew the year was a leap year. Our משנה is about someone who did not know, so he meant the first אדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: You can even say the משנה follows רבי מאיר. This case (the ברייתא) is where the person knew the year was a leap year. That case (the משנה) is where he did not know.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the suggestion from the last step that our משנה follows only רבי יהודה. He shows that רבי מאיר could agree with the משנה, because the two sources deal with different situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר says plain 'Adar' means the second אדר only when the person knew there were two months of אדר that year. Our משנה is about someone who did not know it was a leap year. He only had one 'Adar' in mind, the one that comes right after שבט, which is the first אדר. So the משנה and רבי מאיר do not clash.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You can even say': the source can match even the opinion we thought it went against
'This one... that one': a way of splitting two sources into two different cases
The year is made a leap year, with an extra month of אדר
He knew / he did not know

steps.whatToRemember: Plain 'Adar' means the first אדר when the person did not know it was a leap year. רבי מאיר's view that it means the second אדר applies only when he knew it was a leap year.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two 'הָא's. The first one (he knew) is the ברייתא about documents. The second one (he did not know) is our משנה.
steps.whyThisMatters: אביי shows that what a person knew affects what his words mean. With this answer, the משנה no longer has to follow only one תנא.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר,
phrases.english: Abaye said: You can even say it follows Rabbi Meir,
this one is where he knew that the year was made a leap year,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the ברייתא about dating documents, where רבי מאיר said 'Adar' means the second אדר.

phrases.english: that one is where he did not know.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is our משנה about the vow, where plain 'Adar' means the first אדר.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10's suggestion that the משנה follows only רבי יהודה, by showing it can also fit רבי מאיר.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (הָא בְּ... הָא בְּ...): the two sources deal with different situations, depending on what the person knew.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since רבי מאיר says plain 'Adar' means the second אדר, our משנה, which says it means the first אדר, must follow רבי יהודה and go against רבי מאיר.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר's ruling applies only when the person knew it was a leap year. When he did not know, everyone agrees he meant the first אדר, so the משנה can follow רבי מאיר too.
